Jeremy Clarkson’s harvest ruined by UK heatwave at Diddly Squat Farm
• Written by Chris Martin • Reading duration : 3 minutes·read 46 times
Post on Facebook Post on Flipboard Share on LinkedIn Post on Reddit Share on Telegram Share on X Send through Whatsapp
Jeremy Clarkson has warned that his 1,000-acre Diddly Squat Farm in Oxfordshire faces a devastating harvest as the UK grapples with unprecedented heatwave conditions and drought. On August 9, the television presenter shared a screenshot of a weather forecast showing no rain in sight, declaring his harvest “already f****d” — a stark admission that echoes broader agricultural collapse across the country this summer.
The damage to Clarkson’s farm reflects a national crisis. According to analysis by the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU), the UK’s 2026 cereal and oilseed harvest is on track to be the worst since detailed records began in 1984, with production now forecast at 19.5 million tonnes — surpassing 2020 as the historic low. England experienced its warmest June on record, and England and Wales saw their driest July ever recorded, according to Met Office data cited by Reuters.
The financial toll is staggering. The ECIU estimates that the extreme growing conditions have knocked as much as 2.5 million tonnes off Britain’s expected cereal and oilseed harvest compared to earlier forecasts, costing UK arable farmers up to £390 million in lost revenue. Wheat yields are expected to fall well below the ten-year average at 6.8 tonnes per hectare, with spring barley and oat yields also down significantly.
Clarkson’s struggle is personal but not unique. Speaking at his summer party last year, he admitted that 2025 had been the “second worst recorded ever” for his farm, adding: “I mean, if there are any farmers here, they’d tell you the same thing. Last year, it was the second worst recorded ever, and we think this year is going to be even worse because it just hasn’t rained.” His farm manager Kaleb Cooper has been monitoring moisture levels closely, waiting for any opportunity to harvest before conditions deteriorate further.
The crisis extends far beyond individual farms. The National Farmers’ Union has warned that Britain could face shortages of certain foods due to the drought, and more than 100 organisations wrote to Prime Minister Andy Burnham in late July urging him to make food production a national priority alongside defence and energy. The repeated heatwaves — England is bracing for its fifth in 2026 — have compounded stress on crops already weakened by an exceptionally hot and dry spring.
The ECIU noted that even if yields are revised upward, 2026 is likely to be one of the five worst harvests since records began. This means four of the five worst harvests on record have now occurred this decade, a pattern linked to extreme weather made worse by climate change. For Clarkson and thousands of other UK farmers, the 2026 season represents not just a financial setback but a stark reminder of how vulnerable food production has become in an era of escalating climate extremes.

On August 23, Ukraine will experience a heat wave with temperatures reaching 37 degrees
On August 23, hot weather will continue across Ukraine, although brief showers and thunderstorms are possible in some regions. In the east and southeast, daytime temperatures will reach +35...+37°, while in the north and west it will be cooler—up to +24...+29°.
“At night and in the morning, most of the central and northern regions, as well as the Odesa and Mykolaiv regions, will see brief showers and thunderstorms in some areas; the rest of the country will remain dry during the day,” according to a statement from the Hydrometeorological Center.
The wind will be predominantly northwesterly, 5–10 m/s.
Nighttime temperatures will range from 12–17°, reaching up to 20° in the south and east of the country; during the day, 21–26° in the western, northern, and Vinnytsia regions; 27–32° across the rest of the country; and intense heat of +35–37° in the southeast.
In Kyiv and the surrounding region, brief showers and thunderstorms are forecast in some areas on Sunday night, with no precipitation during the day. The wind will be from the northwest at 5–10 m/s.
In the capital, temperatures will range from +15–17° at night to around +25° during the day; in the Kyiv region, temperatures will range from 12–17° at night to +21–26° during the day.
Source: Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center
According to data from the Boris Sreznevsky Central Geophysical Observatory, the average monthly air temperature in Kyiv in July was 20.8°C, which is 0.5°C below the climatological norm.
The Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center has issued a warning about heat reaching 38° and a fire hazard.

IMD Weather Update Today, 23 August 2026: Delhi, Noida, Gurugram Ghaziabad to witness heavy rainfall, orange alert issued for 25 states
A warning of heavy rain accompanied by thunderstorms has been issued for most districts in both states, which could lead to waterlogging and flood-like situations in low-lying areas.
New Delhi: The monsoon has once again become active across several parts of the country. This sudden change in weather conditions, from the plains to the hilly states, has brought temperatures down in many cities. Delhi-NCR woke up to light rain on Sunday morning. The Meteorological Department has issued orange and yellow alerts for heavy rainfall in several states across North and Central India, including Delhi-NCR, for today.
Since morning, dark clouds have covered the skies over Delhi and surrounding areas, including Noida, Ghaziabad, Gurugram, and Faridabad. Heavy showers accompanied by cool winds are expected, which will lead to a significant drop in temperature and provide much-needed relief from the humid heat. Strong winds have also been blowing since morning.
According to the Meteorological Department, a warning for heavy rain and thunderstorms has been issued today in 25 states
These states include Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Bihar, Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya, Sikkim and Nagaland.
Among the plains states, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are witnessing the most significant impact of the weather.
A warning of heavy rain accompanied by thunderstorms has been issued for most districts in both states, which could lead to waterlogging and flood-like situations in low-lying areas.
The administration has advised people to avoid open spaces during bad weather due to the risk of lightning strikes.
Besides Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, parts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana are also likely to receive heavy to very heavy rainfall.
The monsoon rains have significantly worsened the situation in the hilly states.
Continuous rainfall in several parts of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh has created a serious risk of land subsidence and landslides.
Falling rocks and debris on national highways and connecting roads have brought traffic to a complete halt at several places, leaving hundreds of tourists and local residents stranded.
The Meteorological Department and disaster management authorities have instructed people living along rivers and streams in hilly areas to move to safer locations. They have also urged the general public to avoid travelling to the hills unless absolutely necessary.

The Visayas grid will be placed under yellow alert on Sunday evening, August 23 due to thin reserves as several power plants are unavailable, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said.
In an advisory, the NGCP said the yellow alert will be implemented from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.
The NGCP said that the grid only has an available capacity of 2,516 megawatts despite a peak demand of 2,292 megawatts.
It noted that among the factors for the declaration of yellow alert on the grid include unavailability of two large coal plants in the Visayas. There's also an emergency shutdown of a power plant of Kepco SPC Power Corporation on Saturday due to a suspected boiler tube leak.
The grid operator also said that eight power plants are on forced outage in August 2026, one plant since July, three plants since June, seven plants since May, one plant since March, three plants since 2025, two plants since 2024, two plants since 2023, and one plant since 2021.
Meanwhile, there are nine plants running on derated capacities, resulting to a total of 901.9 megawatts unavailable to the Visayas grid.
A yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the transmission grid’s contingency requirement. —KG, GMA News

Drink water: Drinking plenty of water frequently is vital for those exposed to heat. An individual may produce as much as 2 to 3 gallons of sweat per day. To replenish that fluid you should drink 3 to 4 cups of water every hour.
Take breaks: Taking breaks in a cool shaded area and allowing time for recovery from the heat during the day are effective ways to avoid heat-related illness.
Avoid some beverages: Avoid or limit the use of alcohol and caffeine during periods of extreme heat. Both dehydrate the body.
Stop and rest: If you start to feel symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, weakness or unusual fatigue, rest in a cool shaded area. If symptoms persist or worsen seek immediate medical attention.
Clothing: Whenever possible, wear clothing that provides protection from the sun but allows airflow to the body. Protect your head and shade your eyes when outdoors.
Be prepared: When in the heat be sure to pay extra attention to those you’re with and be sure you know how to call for medical attention.
